p: The building itself is part of the fun. It opened in 1877, paid for by Andrew Barclay Walker, a local brewer and former mayor, and that grand columned front on William Brown Street sets the tone before you have even reached the door. Inside, a few big names are worth seeking out on purpose rather than stumbling past.

Look out for Dante's Dream by Dante Gabriel Rossetti, a huge, dreamy Pre-Raphaelite canvas that stops plenty of people in their tracks. Millais's Isabella is another Pre-Raphaelite favourite, packed with tiny details and a cheeky bit of storytelling if you look at the brothers round the table. Then there is William Frederick Yeames's And When Did You Last See Your Father?, a Civil War scene that many people recognise from school books without ever knowing where it hangs. Older kids tend to love working out what is going on in that one.
The sculpture gallery is a calm spot to pause, and the gallery also hosts the John Moores Painting Prize, a long-running contemporary painting competition, so modern work gets a proper look-in too.

Got an hour? Pick three paintings and give each one a few minutes. Got half a day? Do the Walker, then wander next door to the Central Library's gorgeous Picton Reading Room and finish up at the World Museum. Grab a bite in town afterwards and you have a cracking city day for very little outlay.
